EPPC-CARE's Triplet F1 improved by 2.90 percentage points on average, with a best score of 64.4%. On the human expert evaluation subset, EPPC-CARE and the human expert showed comparable agreement with the reference standard, with differences favoring EPPC-CARE. Discussion: These findings suggest that identifying triplet components (span, code, subcode) sequentially can improve performance across model families while preserving the supporting text behind each identification. EPPC-CARE links the communication code and subcode with the source text (span), supporting human verification of automated annotations in clinical informatics. EPPC-CARE may therefore make larger-scale studies of patient-provider communication more feasible and provide a foundation for human-in-the-loop annotation workflows. Conclusion: EPPC-CARE offers a more reliable and reviewable approach for automated characterization of communication behaviors in secure patient-provider messaging.
papers.comment: 31 pages, 3 figures, 14 tables (includes Appendix / Supplementary Material)

papers.title: Dynamic Task Update Benchmark (DTU-Bench): Evaluating Runtime Task Adaptation in Robotic Manipulation
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies perform well on fixed-instruction robotic manipulation benchmarks, but their ability to adapt to instruction changes during execution remains understudied. We introduce the Dynamic Task Update Benchmark (DTU-Bench), evaluating 40 task revisions across seven update types and three execution stages using LIBERO, a simulated robotic manipulation benchmark. We compare performance when a new instruction is given before execution starts versus during execution, and examine whether the new task instructions are followed. Across 13 representative VLA configurations, average task success is 95.8% on the original object-manipulation tasks, compared with only 1.6% when the instruction changes which object to manipulate during execution. Controlled diagnostics show that policies often complete the original task before the updated one, and that their responses depend on the robot's physical state. We further test whether a simple scripted controller that releases the grasped object and moves the arm back helps robots respond to instruction changes. This improves success from 2% to 38% for π0.5 and from 8% to 48% for DM0.5, but can cause unwanted object motion. These findings reveal limitations that fixed-instruction benchmarks and task-success metrics alone can overlook in evaluating robotic manipulation. Project page: https://dtu-bench.github.io/

papers.title: Diffusion Effects on a Stochastic Amplifier Driven by the Square of a Gaussian Field: Discontinuous Transition to Intermittency
papers.summary: We study the effects of diffusion on the transition to intermittency in stochastic amplification driven by the square of a Gaussian field. The transition is characterized by an order parameter quantifying the spatial uniformity of the amplification. We consider a model in which the diffusion-amplification process is embedded in a random lattice of point absorbers in such a way that the Feynman-Kac formula is restricted to Brownian paths with a range not exceeding a finite cut-off. In this setting, with the Gaussian driving field in a wide class of physical interest, we show that diffusion-induced damping of the amplification is sufficiently strong to change the nature of the transition: from continuous in the absence of diffusion, to discontinuous in the presence of diffusion.
papers.comment: 28 pages, 3 figures, submitted to J. Phys. A: Math. Theor

papers.title: Rational terms and UV counterterms of the SMEFT at next-to-leading order in QCD
papers.summary: We compute the rational terms $R_2$ and the ultraviolet counterterms of the dimension-six Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) at next-to-leading order (NLO) in QCD without any flavour assumption, for complex Wilson coefficients, massive quarks and a general CKM matrix. We also compute the on-shell renormalisation factors of the quark fields in the presence of flavour mixing. We work with an anticommuting $γ_5$ and read closed fermion loops with a single $γ_5$ at the operator insertion. The results, also for common flavour assumptions, are provided in electronic form and in a Mathematica package attached to the paper. We use them to build example models for MadGraph5_aMC@NLO and give NLO predictions for representative processes.

papers.title: AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base
papers.summary: We present AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base, a mixture-of-experts language model with 80 billion total parameters and approximately 3 billion active parameters per token, trained from scratch at Yandex and released under the Apache 2.0 license. The model combines Kimi Delta Attention with full attention, uses Attention Residuals, and is trained with Muon. Training comprises general pretraining on 17.5 trillion tokens, two context-extension stages, and a dedicated stage for reasoning and agentic interaction. We describe the data collection and augmentation pipelines, evaluation protocols, architectural ablations, and scaling-law experiments. We identify the limitations of held-out training loss as a proxy for downstream performance and introduce an auxiliary loss on mixture-of-experts outputs to stabilize training at the predicted learning rate. Domain-specific data selection and augmentation improve factual knowledge, mathematics, and programming skills, while agent trajectories introduced during pretraining improve performance on agentic benchmarks after supervised fine-tuning. In zero-shot reasoning evaluation, the model achieves leading results among open base models of comparable size, with 88.7% pass@8 on IMO-AnswerBench and 82.9% pass@8 on LiveCodeBench v5-v6. To evaluate Russian-language factual knowledge, we introduce and release two benchmarks with their evaluation protocols: WikiWebFacts, which tests short factual questions drawn from encyclopedic sources and search queries, and HardMultiQA, which tests more demanding factual questions inspired by user interactions. Our model scores 86.5% on WikiWebFacts and 67.9% on HardMultiQA, compared with 83.2% and 65.4% for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (284B total and 13B active parameters) and 72.8% and 54.5% for Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-Base (120B total and 12B active parameters), outperforming both larger models on these benchmarks.

papers.title: Lone Wolves and Lattices in Bayesian Matching with Transfers
papers.summary: I study the Lone Wolf and lattice properties of stable outcomes in one-to-one matching with transferable utility and one-sided incomplete information, using the Bayesian stable market states of Liu (2020) and Chen and Hu (2024). With transfers, the wage in a blocking offer screens the worker's types, so it determines both whom the firm attracts and what the firm learns. I show by example that the firm-side and matched-set versions of the Lone Wolf property, as well as the lattice property, can fail even when outcomes are compared under the same information structure. I then assume that each worker's matching value is additively separable in his type and the firm's identity. Under this condition, a firm that is unmatched in some stable outcome earns zero in every stable outcome with the same type profile and information structure. Workers can retain information rents, so the worker-side property can fail. Nevertheless, outside a finite union of affine hyperplanes in the space of firm values, all such stable outcomes leave the same agents unmatched. Whenever they do, the stable payoff vectors form a lattice, and worker-optimal and firm-optimal outcomes exist. The results extend to comonotonicity of relative preferences when posterior beliefs are independent across workers.

papers.title: Dynamics of a Charged Particle on a Conformal Helicoidal Surface
papers.summary: We study the classical and quantum motion of a charged particle on a conformal helicoidal surface embedded in four-dimensional Euclidean space. A uniform ambient magnetic field pulls back to a nonuniform surface field. The cyclic longitudinal coordinate permits an exact transverse reduction. The ordinary helicoid in the same axial field shares the effective potential and the turning points, while the conformal metric increases the physical period at matched energy and longitudinal momentum. We classify the single- and double-well regimes and obtain the exact transverse periods in the two double-well sectors. The periods diverge logarithmically at the separatrix, with twice the leading coefficient above the barrier as below it. The zero-field limit allows transverse escape, and the weak-twist limit is locally free but nonuniform across the surface. Intrinsic quantization gives an exact weighted transverse eigenvalue problem. Fixed-momentum eigenvalues test the harmonic approximation in a central well and resolve the tunneling splittings in a double well.

papers.title: AGLR: Attribute-Guided Latent Refinement for Fine-Grained Humanoid Motion Generation and Editing
papers.summary: Humanoid motion generation must accommodate evolving task requirements, where localized adjustments should satisfy new geometric constraints without disrupting desired motion details. However, language-based control lacks geometric precision, while joint-level constraints require explicit spatial targets. Local geometric constraints are also underdetermined, complicating target satisfaction and source preservation. We present AGLR (Attribute-Guided Latent Refinement), a unified framework for fine-grained humanoid motion generation and editing through source-anchored refinement. A compact geometric interface supports composable, time-varying control of limb extents, torso orientation, and root trajectories. Given a generated or encoded base latent, an Attribute Residual Adapter predicts a single-pass correction, with dual-level supervision enforcing target matching and selective preservation across attributes and motion coordinates. On HumanML3D-G1, AGLR achieves the highest controllable-generation and preservation-constrained editing success rates among evaluated methods. Editing take only 9.1 ms for a cached 500-frame motion, without additional sampling or test-time optimization. Zero-shot evaluation on BONES-SEED-G1 further demonstrates transfer without fine-tuning.

papers.title: Site-Resolved Optical Spectroscopy of Thulium in Solid Argon
papers.summary: We utilize the high resolution of the ground state transition ${}^2\mathrm{F}_{7/2} \leftrightarrow {}^2\mathrm{F}_{5/2}$ in thulium atoms isolated in solid argon to perform excitation-emission spectroscopy. Decomposition of the excitation-emission spectrum reveals 6 absorption-emission profiles, which are attributed to multiple trapping sites in the host matrix. Comparison with vacuum transition energies shows large matrix-induced shifts for $\mathrm{s}\rightarrow\mathrm{p}$ transitions, whereas $\mathrm{f} \rightarrow \mathrm{d}$ transitions remain close to their free-atom energies. A single site exhibiting strong emission at 560nm is investigated and a three-photon excitation pathway is determined as a possible origin of the high energy 560nm light. Additionally, for long-lived levels belonging to the $\mathrm{f}^{12}\mathrm{d}$ configuration, narrow, crystal-field split absorption lines are identified. Matrix effects are important for establishing the mechanism behind the observed spectra and long $\mathrm{f}^{12}\mathrm{d}$ lifetimes.

papers.title: Magnetic Reconfiguration Controls Spin Splitting and Spin-Orbit-Coupled Responses in Compensated Magnets
papers.summary: Compensated magnets provide a versatile platform for spin-dependent electronic and transport phenomena. Here, we show that magnetic reconfiguration, i.e., selective reversal of local moments without changing the underlying crystal structure, can profoundly transform the nonrelativistic spin splitting and spin-orbit-coupled responses of spin-degenerate antiferromagnets (AFMs), altermagnets (AMs), and compensated ferrimagnets (cFIMs). Strikingly, magnetic configurations with nearly degenerate energies can exhibit qualitatively different spin-split band structures and anomalous Hall responses, allowing a small magnetic-energy scale to produce large changes in physical properties. Combining tight-binding models, oriented spin space group analysis, and first-principles calculations, we demonstrate that converting an AM configuration into cFIM states activates staggered onsite-potential contributions to spin splitting, complementing the anisotropic-hopping mechanism of AMs and removing symmetry-enforced degeneracies. Moreover, cFIM symmetry permits an anomalous Hall response at first order in spin-orbit coupling, in contrast to the higher-order or orientation-constrained responses of corresponding AM states. We demonstrate this regime in Mn2Mo3O8, one of 12 cFIM candidates identified in the MAGNDATA database, and further demonstrate its generality by designing cFIMs from collinear AFMs, exemplified by MnGeO3 and Co2Mo3O8. Our results establish magnetic reconfiguration as a powerful symmetry-guided strategy for dramatically reshaping electronic and transport responses in compensated magnets.

papers.title: A Genetic Algorithm Approach to Reconstructing Scalar-Tensor Lagrangians
papers.summary: Recent DESI baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data, combined with cosmic microwave background (CMB) and Type Ia supernovae observations, have been interpreted as evidence for dynamical dark energy whose equation of state crosses the phantom divide $w=-1$. Such a crossing cannot be realized smoothly by a minimally coupled scalar field $\varphi$, but can arise naturally in scalar-tensor theories. We present a data-driven framework that reconstructs the scalar-tensor Lagrangian directly from observations, using a genetic algorithm to evolve the symbolic expressions for the nonminimal coupling $F(\varphi)$ and the scalar potential $U(\varphi)$. Each candidate is evaluated through a forward model that self-consistently determines the expansion history, the effective gravitational coupling, and the growth of structure. Candidates are ranked by a joint likelihood of DESI DR2 BAO, Pantheon+ supernovae calibrated with SH0ES Cepheids, compressed CMB distance priors, and redshift-space distortion measurements of $fσ_8$. We restrict to the unscreened branch of the theory and impose Solar System constraints on the post-Newtonian parameter $γ$ and on the time variation of the gravitational coupling, together with a Big Bang nucleosynthesis bound on its evolution. Across 64 independent runs, the best reconstruction improves the fit relative to $Λ$CDM by $Δχ^2=-16.6$, compared with $Δχ^2=-10.6$ for the CPL dark-energy parametrization. The preferred coupling is well described by $F(\varphi)=c_1\varphi^2+e^{\varphi}(1-c_2\varphi)$. The reconstructed theory shows phantom behavior at $z\gtrsim0.5$, but it remains close to $w=-1$ at low redshift.
papers.comment: V1: 18 pages, 7 figures. The code and data that support the findings of V1 are openly available in the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/Rivillion/ScalarTensor_GA/tree/v1.0.0

papers.title: A Monolithic Fully Eulerian Lattice Boltzmann Framework for Fluid--Structure Interaction with Neo-Hookean Elastic Solids
papers.summary: We present a fully Eulerian, monolithic lattice Boltzmann method for fluid--structure interaction with incompressible neo-Hookean solids at unequal densities, and use it to compute the Turek--Hron FSI2 and FSI3 benchmarks on a single Cartesian grid. A pressure-based kinetic scheme advances the mixture momentum, a polynomial MTHINC reconstruction transports the solid volume fraction with closed-form fluxes, and the left Cauchy--Green tensor gives the elastic stress; all updates are explicit and local. Because the density is transported independently of the populations, two corrections are introduced. A lattice-link correction makes uniform translation an exact discrete solution for any density ratio, which is verified to round-off up to $ρ_s/ρ_f=1000$. A pressure-mode correction, derived from an asymptotic analysis of the scheme, removes the frame-dependent defect that otherwise causes a secular drift of the solid mass. The verification separates the two sources of error: the scheme is second-order accurate towards the diffuse-interface solution at fixed interface thickness, and first-order towards the sharp-interface solution when the thickness scales with the grid, as predicted by an estimate of the interfacial truncation error. The method reproduces a deformable disk in Taylor--Green and lid-driven-cavity flows, and the FSI3 and FSI2 benchmarks at density ratios of one and ten.

papers.title: AFM metrology for 3D high aspect ratio semiconductor structures
papers.summary: Transistors have long been the foundation of the semiconductor industry, with continuous architectural innovations enabling the scaling of integrated circuits while maintaining high performance. Advancements in deposition and lithographic techniques have further expanded design possibilities, while increasing structural complexity demands stricter process control. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) offers a rapid and reliable metrology solution, providing high-resolution measurements and robust statistical analysis of critical parameters. In this work, we present clearly resolved individual profiles of lines and spaces in high aspect ratio (HAR) gate all around FET (GAAFET)-type structures on both the nanosheet (NS) region and in the isolation region between the nanosheets and we present a comprehensive statistical evaluation of their critical dimensions.

papers.title: Know the Design, Pick the Attack: Sentence-Keyed Watermarks for LLMs
papers.summary: A watermark lets the provider of a language model recognise the text its model wrote, which matters more as generated text becomes hard to tell from human writing: provenance underpins academic integrity, the fight against misinformation and new regulation. Providers have started to watermark the text of their models, and to explain how their watermarks work. Explaining a watermark, however, also tells an attacker how to break it, and there are two ways to do so: reword the text to erase the mark, or learn the mark and copy it onto text the model never wrote. Each attack has been studied on its own. We study an attacker that reads the published design to choose between them: it erases the watermarks that are hard to learn and forges the ones that survive rewording. Against it, every existing watermark we compare fails. We propose KeyedLex, which reads its secret key from the grammar of the previous sentence, which rewording changes little, and whose detector does not need to recover the key exactly. It outperforms every watermark we compare on both models we test, losing about half of its signal where the best alternative loses two thirds, at no extra cost in text quality over the best-known watermarks.

papers.title: Nuclear Modification of $π^0$ Production in pO and OO Collisions with ALICE
papers.summary: Energy loss of high-momentum partons is one of the key signatures of the quark--gluon plasma formed in heavy-ion collisions. Through measurements of the nuclear modification factor, $R_{\rm AA}$, where a strong suppression of high-$p_{\rm T}$ particle yields is observed, parton energy loss has been confirmed in Pb--Pb collisions at the LHC. However, in small collision systems, like pp and p--Pb, energy loss has not yet been confirmed. In this contribution, a measurement of the $π^0$ $R_{\rm AA}$ in OO and pO collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.36$ TeV and $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 9.62$ TeV, respectively, is presented. These results are based on the measured $π^0$ $p_{\rm T}$ spectra in OO, pO, and pp collisions using the ALICE electromagnetic calorimeter. The measurement of the $R_{\rm pO}$ allows for precise constraints on cold-nuclear matter effects. In combination with the $R_{\rm OO}$, this allows for a separation of cold and hot nuclear matter contributions and enables a quantitative determination of partonic energy loss in OO collisions. The measurements are compared to theoretical model calculations that include both cold and hot nuclear matter effects.
papers.comment: Contribution to the proceedings for the 13th International Conference on Hard and Electromagnetic Probes of High-Energy Nuclear Collisions (Hard Probes 2026)

papers.title: LetzElPhC: an electron-phonon code for efficient exciton-phonon workflows
papers.summary: We present \texttt{LetzElPhC}, an open-source software package that computes electron-phonon matrix elements from the output of density functional perturbation theory calculations performed with the \texttt{Quantum ESPRESSO} code. By interfacing directly with the \texttt{Yambo} code and exploiting crystal symmetries, \texttt{LetzElPhC} enables a scalable workflow for evaluating exciton-phonon matrix elements while enforcing strict gauge consistency between one-electron Bloch states and Bethe-Salpeter excitonic wave functions across the full Brillouin zone. This symmetry-preserving approach avoids phase ambiguities and significantly reduces both computational costs and memory requirements. To support large-scale simulations on dense momentum grids, the package incorporates Fourier interpolation of dynamical matrices and perturbed Kohn-Sham potentials, accounting for long-range dipole and quadrupole interactions in both two- and three-dimensional materials, combined with multi-level parallelization and efficient parallel I/O. Together, these capabilities seamlessly complement the \texttt{Yambo} code to enable first-principles simulations of phonon-assisted optical spectroscopies, which we demonstrate through applications to resonant Raman scattering in monolayer $\text{WSe}_2$ and phonon-assisted luminescence in cubic AgBr.
papers.comment: Supplementary information can be found at https://github.com/muralidhar-nalabothula/MyPapers/blob/main/LetzElPhC_paper/SI/agbr_phonon_viewer.html

papers.title: StePPO: Adaptive Step-Size Control for Initial-Value Problems Using Proximal Policy Optimisation
papers.summary: ODE solvers are used to model, simulate, and analyse continuous-time systems found in many signal processing applications. Time integration of these initial-value problems is traditionally performed using adaptive embedded Runge--Kutta methods. For proper time-step selection, adaptive solvers accept or reject each candidate step according to a local error estimate. Their efficiency is therefore controlled by the rule that selects the next step size. Classical proportional--integral--derivative (PID) controllers are computationally inexpensive per decision and reliable, but their reactive design can lead to costly numerical solves near stiff transitions. We formulate step-size selection for parametrised IVPs as a Markov decision process and train a continuous-action policy using proximal policy optimisation. The policy processes its observation signals using a deep network while maintaining the embedded solver logic. We evaluate on a decay function, the Van der Pol system, and the Brusselator system at matched tolerances, and compare against a standard PID controller and a multi-scale DeepONet network. We find that the proposed learned policy remains within prescribed error tolerances while reducing the required number of solve steps by up to 60%, achieving a wall-clock time reduction of 58%, for both in- and out-of-distribution settings.
papers.comment: Preprint for ICASSP & IEEE Open Journal of Signal Processing submission

papers.title: FlyingStart: Learned Cross-Token Warm Starts for Fixed-Point Decoding in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
papers.summary: Recurrent-depth language models generate each token by iterating a shared block of layers until its hidden state converges. Inference methods for these models decide when to stop the iteration, yet every token still starts from random noise and pays the full cost of converging. We show that where the iteration starts is a second, independent lever. A token's fixed point is predictable from the state at which the previous token stopped, after a learned change of coordinates, and we introduce FlyingStart, a linear warm start that is fitted in closed form on the frozen model and costs under 5% of one loop. The iteration and its stopping rule are unchanged, so the exit criterion certifies the same distance to the fixed point from any start: a better start removes loops at unchanged accuracy. On Huginn-0125, FlyingStart matches the accuracy of the strongest training-free baseline with 14--19% fewer decoding layers, raises batched throughput by 16--18% in two serving engines, and adds a further 10--14% on top of self-speculative decoding. A contraction analysis predicts the number of loops saved on all four models we study, including one where the prediction was recorded before any evaluation, and token by token on Huginn, and it identifies when a warm start pays off: the saving grows with the number of loops a model needs to converge.

papers.title: Where Does the Asymmetry Enter? Staging a Fairness Audit Across a Fused Multimodal Moderation Pipeline
papers.summary: Almost every short-video upload now passes through a classifier that fuses video, speech, and on-screen text into one decision about whether it may be seen. It moderates every language community on the platform at once, and fairness across them is judged, if at all, from one accuracy score. That score is compatible with error falling almost entirely on one language group. An audit that goes looking reads the model's decisions, the last stage of a long pipeline and the one whose test has the fewest items. We ask where in a fused pipeline a subgroup asymmetry can be detected at all: in what the classifier may read, in what its branches encode, or in what it decides. We answer this with a post-hoc audit of a published TikTok classifier, holding all three stages to one significance standard using only its logged decisions, labels, and pre-fusion features, with source language as the subgroup axis. The asymmetry is significant at the stage deciding what the model may read, and again in what the text branch encodes. At the earlier stage, a language-blind cap admits less of a Vietnamese clip than an English one, for reasons of segmentation, not verbosity. The asymmetry is undetectable at the decision, where the smallest subgroup leaves twelve items to test. An audit reading only decisions looks where its evidence is thinnest; the same test staged upstream recovers a disparity the decision-level view returns as noise.
papers.comment: Accepted at the 40th Pacific Asia Conference on Language, Information and Computation (PACLIC 40)

papers.title: Fast Fluid Antenna Multiple Access: Exact Analysis and Fixed-Aperture Asymptotics
papers.summary: In this paper, we investigate the interference-limited outage performance of fast fluid antenna multiple access (FAMA), in which the receive port is selected according to the instantaneous symbol-based signal-to-interference energy ratio. For any positive-definite spatial covariance matrix and an arbitrary finite number of candidate ports, we show that constant-modulus multiuser interference admits an exact reduction to the comparison of two independent correlated exponential random vectors. This representation leads to a nonnegative double multi-index series for the outage probability, a recursive coefficient evaluation, and a certified truncation-error bound. We then study the distinct asymptotic regime where the number of candidate ports goes to infinity while the physical aperture remains unchanged, assuming exponential spatial correlation. For this model, we derive an explicit finite-port series requiring no numerical integration, and characterize continuous port selection through a convergent one-dimensional series for arbitrary thresholds. The analysis further yields an exact expression relating the maximum supportable number of users to the antenna aperture size and target outage probability. Numerical results validate the finite-port and asymptotic analyses, and illustrate that given sufficient aperture size, a user utilizing fast FAMA can overcome a massive number of interferers for decent communication performance.

papers.title: Backpropagation as Dirac-bracket dynamics of dissipative training
papers.summary: Gradient-based training of a parametric model is the motion of a damped particle in the potential set by the loss. Using the Bateman-Galley doubling of the degrees of freedom, which gives dissipative systems an action principle, we write gradient flow, the heavy-ball method and Nesterov's accelerated gradient method as Hamiltonian systems. We show that, within this Hamiltonian description, backpropagation is Dirac evolution. The activations of a feed-forward network are treated as coordinates of phase space, and the layer equations as constraints. These constraints are second class for every architecture, and Hamilton's equations with the resulting Dirac bracket reproduce training with the exact gradient of the loss, although the Hamiltonian contains only the cost of the network output. The Dirac bracket of an activation with the momenta of the parameters is its Jacobian, the inverse of the constraint matrix contains both the forward and the reverse modes of automatic differentiation, and the errors propagated by backpropagation are the Lagrange multipliers of the layer constraints: the constraint forces of a kinematic chain under the load of the cost. These results hold in the full doubled phase space, not only in the physical limit. The network's part of the constraint algebra is the same for every optimizer, Nesterov's look-ahead adds one layer of momentum-dependent constraints that couple the two copies of the doubled system, and gradient flow is obtained by constructing the Dirac bracket in stages. We confirm these statements numerically to machine precision and train a network by integrating the Dirac flow of its constraints, with no backward pass in the computation.
papers.comment: 14 pages, 1 figure. Submitted to Physical Review E

papers.title: Fuel as Identity: Authenticating Inter-Satellite Laser Links after Total Key Compromise
papers.summary: Optical inter-satellite links form the backbone of entire constellations in low Earth orbit, yet their security rests on keys alone. When an attacker obtains every key of a satellite, no secret is left to authenticate it again. Existing fixes fail, since ground rekeying encrypts new keys under the leaked ones, and post-compromise protocols assume an authenticated start. As a remedy, the satellite's orbit can take over as the trust anchor. The attacker then needs an impostor satellite that blocks and retransmits the beam, a chord beneath the curved orbit. Hence, the blocking point lies off free fall and costs the impostor continuous thrust. We formalize this position-gated adversary and prove, for satellites on a shared circular orbit, a tight lower bound on the propellant cost in delta-v of a point-mass craft that keeps blocking, however it moves. We present OrbitLock, a history-chained protocol that combines this position gate with ML-KEM. Each link authenticates on its own, and we sketch how combining links forces an impostor onto every link. Once the chain outlasts an impostor's propellant, every key back to the first is authenticated retroactively. A satellite thus needs no crosslink key before launch, so none can leak in the supply chain. The same mechanism heals the link after total key compromise, even without compromise awareness. A passive attacker is shut out at the next round, whereas an active one splits the chains and is exposed once its propellant runs out. The chain can then heal after an operator reset. As a result, every Starlink satellite has a partner on whose link a CubeSat-class impostor runs out of propellant in about two days. This holds against one rigid craft per link running the best attack we know, if each terminal enforces a 1 km exclusion zone, while the protocol only uses under 0.02% of the link.

papers.title: Ultralight Dark Matter Spectrum with Gravitational Focusing and Doppler Motion
papers.summary: Ultralight dark matter can produce signals in experiments through its couplings with the Standard Model particles. The resulting signal spectrum is determined by the phase-space distribution of dark matter, which encodes information about its production mechanism and the history of the local universe. However, the local environmental effects can modify the observed spectrum and should be included in signal modeling to avoid biased parameter estimates. In this work, we investigate how the gravitational focusing by Sun and the Doppler effect due to the detector's motion modify the signal spectrum and affect inferring the underlying dark matter parameters. We analytically estimate the signal significance and perform Bayesian analysis on simulated data to demonstrate their impact.

papers.title: Uphill Diffusion in Yukawa Plasmas
papers.summary: In a fluid mixture of many species an individual species can diffuse toward higher concentration without any external driving force because its flux is coupled to the gradients of other components. Such `uphill diffusion' is well known in the chemical and metallurgy literature but to our knowledge has not been studied for strongly coupled plasmas in neutron star and white dwarf interiors. We have previously developed a semi-analytic diffusion model that accurately predicts diffusion coefficients of individual species in a mixture in equilibrium. Uphill diffusion allows us to test this model out of equilibrium, and also test a generalized Darken relation for predicting diffusivities. We derive an analytic theory and compare to three-component molecular dynamics simulations and find very good agreement. This provides a novel out-of-equilibrium test of the generalization of our diffusion model to arbitrary multi-component mixtures.

papers.title: Solitons as conversion events in quadratic crystals
papers.summary: In a $χ^{(2)}$ crystal with temporal walk-off and negligible dispersion, signal, idler and pump pulses obey the integrable three-wave interaction. For a pump of intermediate group velocity we describe each soliton as a conversion event: the fusion of a signal--idler pair into a pump pulse, or the decay of a pump pulse, at a definite depth in the crystal. The asymptotic $\mathrm{sech}$ pulses, usually treated with three separate $2\times2$ scattering problems, are the legs of the event, a single pole of the $3\times3$ problem. For one event we give the conversion curve in closed form and the minimum crystal length; for several events, the rule by which they displace each other. A pump pulse is unstable, and its growing mode is the tail of a decay event: a seed carrying a fraction $\varepsilon$ of the photons along this mode makes the pulse decay after $Γ^{-1}\ln(c_+/\varepsilon)$, with $Γ$ the conversion rate and $c_+$ of order one. Unmatched signal and idler pulses form the resonance of Kaup, Reiman and Bers; we show that it is a fusion followed by a decay, each within a conversion length, and give its pump photon number in closed form. Since the delay between the input pulses sets the depth of the vertex, these quantities can be read on the output face of a single crystal; we give the scales for periodically poled KTiOPO$_4$.

papers.title: Decision-Aligned Value Learning for Selective Adoption of EEG Fusion in Human-Robot Collaboration
papers.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) captures neural activity associated with human perception and decision-making. It provides human-robot collaboration (HRC) systems with measurable evidence for event recognition, situation assessment, and action preparation. External sensing cannot easily provide such evidence. However, the quality and complementarity of this evidence vary across samples, and existing EEG fusion methods do not explicitly determine when EEG improves a prediction. We therefore framed selective EEG use as a sample-wise incremental-value estimation problem and proposed Value Estimation and Constraint-Aware Triage for Adoption (VECTA). VECTA separates the generation of an EEG-informed Fusion prediction from the decision about whether it should replace the existing Base prediction. The framework uses system gain to quantify the loss reduction from Base to Fusion and matching gain to assess whether benefits arise from sample-matched EEG. A signed-value learner estimates system gain from decision-time evidence and prioritizes high-value Fusion outputs under budget constraints. Cross-subject evaluations on three HRC datasets showed that matched Fusion outperformed shuffled controls. Estimated gains tracked realized gains, with Spearman correlations of 0.347-0.612 and positive-gain areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) of 0.708-0.842. Under budget constraints, VECTA reduced Brier loss and harmful Fusion adoption and achieved the highest mean normalized AUBC across three datasets among the selective-decision methods evaluated. Validation on three external multi-modal datasets showed that VECTA could be applied directly as a post-hoc decision layer to task-specific predictors without retraining. These results show that selective Fusion adoption can translate the uneven utility of EEG into system-level gains.

papers.title: Travelling-Wave-Based Protection of DC Hubs in Bipolar HVDC Grids
papers.summary: This paper presents a stationary wavelet transform (SWT)-based method for DC fault detection and classification in a three-terminal bipolar modular multilevel converter (MMC)-based HVDC system with a dedicated metallic return (DMR). The system incorporates DC switching stations (DCSSs) with interconnected DC circuit breakers (DCCBs). The method uses line-mode voltage wavelet detail energy for fault detection and wavelet detail energy derived from pole voltages and DMR current for fault classification, distinguishing pole-to-pole, pole-to-ground, and pole-to-DMR faults. Its performance is evaluated using a real-time hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) platform integrating an real-time digital simulator (RTDS) with embedded processing hardware. Busbar and cable faults with varying fault types, resistances, and locations are investigated. The results demonstrate the feasibility of real-time implementation and characterize the effects of fault location and travelling-wave propagation on transient energy and protection response time. The effectiveness of pole-voltage and DMR-current detail energy features in distinguishing fault types is also evaluated.

papers.title: Black hole entropy from angular holonomies of Sine-Gordon soliton lattices in AdS$_3$
papers.summary: We construct boundary conditions for AdS$_3$ gravity that realize Sine-Gordon dynamics. For a periodic soliton lattice at fixed winding, we relate the angular holonomy to the exact acoustic dispersion by continuing the Bloch momentum through the zero-frequency band edge associated with rigid translation of the lattice. For suitable embedding angles, the stable vacuum has a regular BTZ geometry. When only one chiral sector carries winding, we construct a family whose asymptotic region extends to a BTZ black hole. As the spectral parameter of the winding sector tends to the corresponding band edge, the black hole approaches extremality. The leading correction to the extremal entropy is linear in the Hawking temperature defined with respect to laboratory time, with a coefficient inversely proportional to the sound velocity of the lattice. The same inverse-velocity dependence appears in the low-temperature entropy of one-dimensional quantum fluids.

papers.title: vSFT: Learning to Verbally Tune Agents at Test Time
papers.summary: Large language model agents are increasingly improved via agentic reinforcement learning, which can be on-policy but suffers from expensive rollouts and sparse rewards, limiting its application at test time. In this paper, we present a verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (vSFT) framework that enables the conjunction of dense feedback in natural language and weight updates at test time. Specifically, our vSFT forms a closed loop between an agent and a supervisor via a hypernetwork, in which the supervisor generates verbal supervision from the agent's failed trajectories, and the hypernetwork converts that supervision into low-rank weight updates to tune the agent. We validate that this test-time in-parameter evolving process outperforms both its in-context counterparts and prevalent reinforcement learning methods. In particular, our vSFT using Qwen3-4B outperforms GRPO and Reflexion by 8.7% and 13.9% in success rate on ALFWorld, and by 4.8% and 18.2% on WebShop, respectively. We believe that learning how to adapt a model, rather than an adapted model, offers a promising path towards more capable agents that improve themselves.

papers.title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Medical Question Answering on ESC Cardiology Guidelines: Evaluation and Retrieval Optimization
papers.summary: Background: Large language models produce hallucinations in medical question answering (QA). Verify-and-revise pipelines that check atomic claims against retrieved guideline evidence are a standard mitigation, but evaluations almost universally treat the verifier's output as ground truth, an assumption rarely tested. Objective: To measure, claim by claim against human judgement, how such a pipeline fails in a guideline-grounded clinical setting. Methods: We built a dataset of 160 questions (100 patient vignettes from 89 de-identified cases, 60 fact-based) over four recent ESC cardiology guidelines, all approved by a practising internist, and a retrieval corpus of 627 hand-verified guideline records at two chunk granularities. A five-stage pipeline was run under four retrieval configurations and three independent runs (1920 arm-runs); all 606 first-pass refuted claims were manually audited, an independent judge re-judged 906 decisions, and the expert blindly reviewed 100 accepted claims. Results: Only 44.7-50.6% of flagged claims were true hallucinations. Correction loops converged in 85.2-95.1% of cases, yet 35% of genuine final errors were introduced by correction. Single-run true-hallucination recall was 35.6-41.2%, the three-run union 71-80%; verifier agreement was moderate (kappa = 0.505). The blind probe estimated the accepted-claim miss rate at 3.2% (95% CI 0.7-6.7%). Final genuine-error rate: 1.7% of answers. Conclusion: Claim-level verification reduces hallucinated content by an order of magnitude, but verifier reliability, not generation, is the limiting factor and must be measured, not assumed.
papers.comment: 29 pages, 3 figures, 12 tables. Dataset and code: https://github.com/ilkinmasimov/esc-hallucination-qa

papers.title: Reading the Room with AI: FOMC Deliberation and Growth-at-Risk
papers.summary: Macro-at-Risk models forecast the growth distribution from public data; policy is set by a committee arguing over their meaning. From FOMC Minutes, public three weeks after each meeting, we add several dimensions of deliberation to a growth quantile model on FRED-MD's 123 series. Only disagreement present in the discussion but absent from the vote lowers out-of-sample loss by 4-6 percent, chiefly in the center, beyond professional, staff and Committee forecasts. Much of deliberation's informational value lies in the recorded discussion itself, and in the disagreement it reveals, rather than in the risk assessments the Committee chooses to state.

papers.title: DocSEAM: Bidirectional Cross-Page Encoding for Multi-Page Document Understanding
papers.summary: Multi-page document vision-language models encode each page independently, creating a feature-level discontinuity at page boundaries: visual tokens are formed without access to content on adjacent pages, and the language model must reason over these page representations formed in isolation. We introduce DocSEAM (Document Selective Enrichment via Anchored Masking), a lightweight module inserted between a pretrained vision encoder and the language model that injects the inductive bias of local cross-page context into visual representations. For each page, DocSEAM forms a local triplet with its two neighbors, applies center-anchored masked self-attention with directional salience gates to fuse information from neighbor pages, and returns only the enriched center-page tokens, leaving the visual token count unchanged. After a supervised cross-page warm-up and multi-page fine-tuning with DocSEAM frozen, our 9B-parameter model achieves state-of-the-art results among the evaluated open-weight models of up to 10B parameters on five multi-page document VQA benchmarks. We further show that under controlled re-pagination, DocSEAM reduces sensitivity to boundary placement and improves cross-page span localization

papers.title: Decision-Focused Learning for Multistage Stochastic Programs, with Application to Power Network Repair Scheduling
papers.summary: Multistage stochastic programs (MSPs) with discrete decisions are hard to solve due to the curse of dimensionality, non-convex value functions, and scenario trees that grow exponentially with the horizon. We develop a decision-focused learning (DFL) framework for MSPs in which a neural network predicts scores for the part of the decision that drives the state transition. Under structural conditions that make this sub-decision enter the stage objective linearly, the network is trained on labels from offline single-scenario problems, using the Fenchel-Young loss with perturbed optimizers, which need only an optimization oracle. We apply the framework to repair scheduling in power networks under stochastic, time-varying component failures, with and without a per-stage repair budget. On a synthetic 5-bus network and on the IEEE 14-bus network at two repair-cost scales, the learned and baseline policies are compared on common evaluation paths. Without the budget, DFL is the cheapest policy on the 5-bus network; on the 14-bus network it does not outperform a near-sighted model-predictive control (MPC) baseline, but it beats repairing every failed component at the higher scale. Under a binding budget, DFL is the cheapest policy evaluated on both networks and at both scales, 14% to 23% below the next-best policy. On the 5-bus network, the mean cost of DFL is 1.7% (without the budget) and 1.8% (with it) above the exact optimum computed by dynamic programming. Within days of computation, sample average approximation yields costlier policies than DFL and the repair-everything heuristic, and stochastic dual dynamic integer programming remains far from convergence. DFL computes its decisions about as fast as the trivial heuristics and orders of magnitude faster than MPC. Since these conditions are not specific to power networks, the framework extends to other MSPs that share this structure.

papers.title: Northstar: Efficient Verifiable Negacyclic Polynomial Arithmetic with Applications to Encrypted Lattice-based Multi-Asset ERC-20 and Verifiable FHE
papers.summary: Lattice-based cryptography can be used to construct a variety of post-quantum cryptographic schemes, ranging from standard cryptographic primitives such as digital signatures and encryption, to fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). However, the verification of correct lattice computations remains relatively expensive, particularly for computationally intensive FHE operations and for resource-constrained environments such as on-chain verification via smart contracts. We propose Northstar, an efficient technique for proving negacyclic arithmetic natively. When integrated with existing STARK proving frameworks, Northstar achieves the best overall performance across prover time, verifier time, and proof size compared to prior state-of-the-art approaches for verifiable FHE constructions. Furthermore, Northstar is used to construct the first verifiable encrypted multi-asset (~ 1000 assets) variant of ERC-20 that is efficiently verifiable by a smart contract, and is practically deployable in the current blockchain ecosystem.
papers.comment: Extended version of a paper accepted to Financial Cryptography and Data Security 2027 (FC 2027)

papers.title: Large-scale fission properties with BSkG3 I : fission paths and spontaneous fission half-lives
papers.summary: We present our first large-scale analysis of nuclear fission properties based on the BSkG3 energy density functional. Building on the model's unprecedented agreement with ground state observables and fission data in the actinide region, we survey nearly 3300 nuclei with $80\leq Z\leq118$, spanning the region between the predicted proton and neutron drip lines. We calculate thousands of potential energy surfaces that explicitly account for triaxial and octupole deformations. We determine the corresponding least-action fission paths using microscopic collective inertias derived consistently from BSkG3 and calculate spontaneous fission (SF) half-lives within the semiclassical WKB approximation. Our results reveal a rich diversity of fission path topologies, extending well beyond the conventional two-humped picture commonly adopted in reaction codes, and a wide variety of nuclear shapes along these paths, highlighting the limitations of exploring only one collective degree of freedom. In particular, triaxiality affects not only inner barriers in the actinide region but also outer barriers and single barriers in several regions of the superheavy nuclei. Our predicted SF half-lives follow trends similar to those of previous large-scale studies, although significant differences emerge near the neutron drip line. The resulting dataset, including fission barriers, SF half-lives, and saddle-point nuclear level densities, is available has been incorporated into the TALYS reaction code and the BRUSLIB repository. It provides a microscopic foundation for nuclear reaction calculations and astrophysical applications, particularly rapid neutron-capture simulations, which require reliable fission properties of nuclei far from the valley of stability.

papers.title: Structure-preserving finite element method for the 2D MHD-$α$ turbulence system
papers.summary: We propose a structure-preserving finite element method for the two-dimensional MHD-$α$ turbulence model, which filters the transport velocity at a length $α$ while retaining the ideal invariants of the original MHD equations, with the energy replaced by an $α$-dependent energy. The scheme preserves mass conservation and the magnetic Gauss law pointwise and satisfies discrete dissipation laws for the energy, the cross helicity and the mean square magnetic potential, which reduce to exact conservation in the ideal limit. The discrete systems are solved by an augmented Lagrangian preconditioner with monolithic geometric multigrid, observed to be robust with respect to the filter width $α$ and the Reynolds numbers, and to the mesh size for small time steps. The scheme converges at the optimal rates and agrees with a Fourier pseudo-spectral direct simulation of the original MHD equations at the large scales. In under-resolved flows, the unfiltered scheme has no numerical dissipation and accumulates energy at the grid scale. Filtering relieves this accumulation and a larger $α$ gives a more compact spectrum. Long-time simulations reproduce selective decay, including relaxation toward the Arnold-type bound and the inverse cascade of the mean square potential.

papers.title: Passive Fault-Tolerant Antenna Stabilisation for Ship-to-Shore Communication
papers.summary: Directional ship-to-shore radio links require continuous antenna alignment with the shore station, while vessel heave induces variations in antenna height above the sea surface, thereby altering the multipath interference governing the received power. In conventional stabilised gimbals, attitude compensation is provided, whereas fault tolerance is rarely considered. To address these limitations, a passive fault-tolerant control scheme is proposed, whereby the antenna is mounted on a ship-mounted six-degree-of-freedom manipulator, enabling simultaneous regulation alignment and antenna height. Through feedback linearisation, the manipulator dynamics are decoupled into perturbed integrators, each controlled by a multi-barrier adaptive super-twisting sliding-mode controller. The nested barriers are associated with the performance regions of fault-tolerant control, such that inter-sample barrier crossings under discrete-time implementation lead to graceful performance degradation rather than loss of confinement. Under simulated conditions, superior pointing and heave accuracy is achieved compared with single-barrier designs, for which either precision or confinement is compromised.
papers.comment: Submitted to the 13th IFAC Symposium on Fault Detection, Supervision and Safety for Technical Processes (SAFEPROCESS 2027), 6 pages, 6 figures

papers.title: Recoverability policy editing for closed-loop safety in autonomous driving
papers.summary: Autonomous driving powered by neural network models lacks safety guarantees. We propose a state-level policy editing technique that guarantees closed-loop safety under recoverable disturbances while reusing the model's existing driving capabilities. Closed-loop safety means that the vehicle remains free of collisions at all future times. We introduce the concept of policy recoverability to characterize whether a vehicle can safely return to the original policy's feasible set in finite time. Our method identifies states that are unsafe in the long term under the original policy but recoverable, and selectively edits policy outputs within this region. The vehicle corrects its actions upon entering this region and resumes the original policy upon recovery. Closed-loop simulations on nuPlan urban driving scenarios show a 48% reduction in safety incidents under the original policy while largely preserving its driving performance.

papers.title: Optimization of a Locally Shielded 16-Channel Transmit Array for Human Brain MRI at 10.5 T via Electromagnetic/Circuit Co-Simulation and Parallel Transmission Strategies
papers.summary: Modern neuroimaging and neuroscience increasingly demand high spatial and temporal resolution, driving the use of ultrahigh-field (7 T and above) MRI for improved signal-to-noise ratio. Realizing this advantage depends critically on advanced radiofrequency (RF) and gradient technologies, particularly multi-channel transmit arrays and high-performance head-gradient systems. In integrated systems, a local RF shield must provide sufficient field confinement while preserving transmit performance and minimizing sensitivity to nearby conductive structures. In this work, we sought to optimize a locally shielded 16-channel transmit RF array for human neuroimaging at 10.5 T using electromagnetic/circuit co-simulation combined with parallel-transmission strategies. Candidate transmit-array and RF-shield configurations were evaluated before and after gradient-shield integration to identify a configuration with suitable RF transmit and shielding performance for the integrated system. The results show that no single standalone metric, including static RF shimming performance, dynamic parallel transmission (pTx) performance, or external-field leakage, reliably predicts robustness after gradient-shield integration. Progressive screening identified the aligned loop-folded dipole (LFD) array combined with a compact cylindrical shield featuring a conical top and three windows (160-mm radius and 70-mm window length) as the final configuration. Without RF-circuit retuning, the selected design maintained external-field leakage below 1% and after gradient shield integration achieved whole-brain excitation coefficient of variation (CoV) of approximately 27% with static RF shimming and 9% with dynamic pTx. Experimental validation of the unshielded LFD array showed good agreement between simulated and measured B1+ efficiency distributions, with a normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE) of approximately 8%.

papers.title: Funding Landscape of Early-Career Scientists: A Perspective from the AGU SPA Early Career Leadership Advisory Committee
papers.summary: Like researchers across many scientific fields, early-career researchers in heliophysics face a critical transition from supervised research to independent scientific inquiry. However, the funding landscape that should support this transition is fragmented and unpredictable. Here we examine the current funding opportunities available to early-career researchers in heliophysics alongside the historical experiences of established scientists who navigated similar transitions. We catalog the major U.S. federal programs targeting early-career space physicists, documenting their eligibility constraints, selection rates, and accessibility. Access varies with career stage, appointment type, citizenship requirements, and solicitation schedules, and selection rates can swing sharply: the NASA Heliophysics Early Career Investigator Program (ECIP) selected 28% of proposals in 2022 but only 6% in 2024. To provide historical context, we collected survey responses from 30 researchers whose PhDs span 1972-2016 and conducted eight interviews with mid- and senior-career researchers. Most respondents viewed the present funding environment as more difficult than their own early careers, identifying predictability of opportunity, not ease, as what enabled earlier generations to build independence. Salary support alone does not guarantee opportunities to develop scientific leadership; accessible PI awards and real responsibility within collaborative projects can both contribute to that development. We recommend predictable, adequately sized grant programs for early-career principal investigators, transparent reporting of selection statistics across all early-career programs, continued use of dual-anonymous peer review, and named leadership roles for early-career researchers within large projects.
papers.comment: 15 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Submitted to Perspectives of Earth and Space Scientists (AGU)

papers.title: Producing and Measuring Circularly Polarized X-rays: A Jones and Mueller-Stokes Treatment of Crystal Phase Plates
papers.summary: Converting a linearly polarized X-ray beam into a circularly polarized one, and then verifying the polarization state actually delivered, are standard operations at synchrotron radiation facilities. The key optical element is a quarter-wave plate (QWP), a birefringent crystal that introduces a 90-degree (quarter-wavelength) phase retardation between the two orthogonal components of the electric field. This paper presents a self-contained theoretical treatment of X-ray polarization optics. We first establish the Jones and Mueller-Stokes formalisms and their connection via the Pauli matrices, fixing the sign and handedness conventions explicitly and reconciling them with those used elsewhere in the literature. From there we derive the Jones and Mueller matrices of a general retarder at an arbitrary orientation angle chi (including the QWP that converts horizontal linear polarization into circular polarization of either handedness) and of linear polarizers, and describe the experimental Stokes polarimetry protocol used at synchrotron beamlines. These results are then combined to treat the general crystal phase plate, characterized by two complex reflection (or transmission) amplitudes r_s and r_p, obtaining the degree of circular polarization delivered for an arbitrary incident beam as a function of chi and the phase retardation delta. Finally, we turn to the practical implementation of these elements with perfect-crystal diffraction: the residual polarization impurity of a Brewster-angle polarizer and the role of ray tracing in evaluating it, and the choice of diffraction geometry (Bragg or Laue, diffracted or transmitted beam) for obtaining a significant, controllable phase shift. The formalism presented here is the mathematical background of the treatment of polarization in the ray-tracing code SHADOW4.

papers.title: MIMOS: A Toolbox for Multivariable Modal Identification
papers.summary: Accurate and physically interpretable models are essential for the analysis and control of complex multivariable systems. This paper presents the Multivariable Identification of Modal Optical and mechatronic Systems (MIMOS) toolbox, an open-source MATLAB toolbox for identifying physical modal models from measured multivariable frequency response functions. The two-stage approach first estimates an additive input-output model from measured frequency responses and subsequently recovers the physical modal structure through information-weighted projection. MIMOS implements this approach in a practical and scalable workflow combining frequency response preprocessing, interactive modal initialization and refinement, and support for proportional and general viscous damping. Experimental results on a publicly available $6\times8$ vibration isolation benchmark and a $7\times17$ prototype wafer stage demonstrate the capability of MIMOS to effectively handle identification problems involving thousands of parameters and estimate accurate, minimal-order physical modal models.

papers.title: Unveiling gauge-invariant on-chip phases from light intensity
papers.summary: Physics-informed digital twins fitted to output powers increasingly program photonic processors, but these powers do not fix the implemented phase, which determines how light from different inputs interferes. Here we show that a twin trained on intensities alone predicts the gauge-invariant phase of programmed transformations, and that this prediction can be used to program the phase. On a $12\times12$ mesh, with phases measured by interference protocols formed by the mesh itself, intensity-only and phase-aware programs from random starts reach the same intensity fidelity but phase fidelities of 0.690 and 0.996, both as predicted by the twin. The prediction holds for blocks up to $10\times10$. With coherent inputs, the programmed phase determines the outputs: phase-aware programming reduces the direction-of-arrival error of an on-chip Butler matrix from 29 degrees to 2.0 degrees. Power measurements alone thus yield a phase-calibrated model of the mesh, without phase data in training or optics beyond the chip.

papers.title: Decoupling the clocks of learning and computing in spiking neural networks
papers.summary: Biological intelligence thrives on minimal power despite its noisy, imperfect components, with neurons that communicate through voltage spikes. Brain-inspired computing seeks to bring such efficiency to real devices, which requires training methods tailored to them. The standard way to train spiking neural networks, backpropagation through time, computes weight updates through every step of a simulated device, so faithful or long simulations can make training costly and unstable. Here we show that spiking networks can learn reliably and efficiently by decoupling the clock of learning from that of computing. Our method, ChronoProp, calculates weight updates from each neuron's spike counts in fixed time bins using its measured input-output function. Compared with backpropagation through time, ChronoProp reaches similar accuracy in image classification, with about 3 times less training time and 20 times less memory at the finest timestep tested, and up to 10 times fewer spikes. On spoken-word benchmarks, ChronoProp is far more accurate in recurrent networks at fine timesteps, and with simple, hardware-compatible techniques it approaches the best published models. These networks also tolerate simulated hardware defects and limitations better than those trained with backpropagation through time. Therefore, ChronoProp enables stable and efficient training in simulations close to the continuous time of analog hardware.

papers.title: AgentLens: Graph-guided Security Auditing for LLM-based Agents
papers.summary: LLM-based agents are emerging as a key paradigm for automating software engineering by coupling LLM-driven decision-making with external tools, files, APIs, and execution environments. However, weaknesses in agent implementations and insecure interactions between the agent and external resources can lead to severe consequences, including remote code execution, arbitrary file access, SQL injection, and data leakage. This makes pre-deployment auditing essential for systematically identifying implementation weaknesses and validating whether they can manifest as concrete security risks in realistic agent workflows. Existing approaches either focus on specific vulnerability classes or lack the capability to validate whether identified static weaknesses correspond to executable exploits. In this paper, we propose AgentLens, a systematic auditing framework for LLM-based agents. AgentLens analyzes the target agent's implementation, component interactions, and built-in defenses, and organizes them into an Audit Knowledge Graph that captures how these factors interact to expose potential security risks. Based on this graph, AgentLens derives candidate attack paths, generates path-specific validation payloads, and constructs realistic multi-turn audit scenarios that place these payloads in task-relevant contexts to validate whether suspected risks manifest as security-violating behaviors during execution. Across five widely-used agent applications, each with over 24,000 GitHub stars, AgentLens identifies 44 vulnerabilities, and every vulnerability is validated by being triggered during execution. Compared with the state-of-the-art approach (AgentFuzz), AgentLens detects 3.67$\times$ more vulnerabilities. To date, 12 reported issues have been assigned CVE IDs.

papers.title: BADGERS: Bayesian Adaptive Graph-Guided Errors-in-Variables Regression Solution for Structured High-Dimensional Data
papers.summary: Knowledge-guided learning methods that incorporate biological graph information into the analysis of structured high-dimensional data, such as genomic data, can improve variable selection and prediction accuracy while yielding more interpretable results. However, these methods typically assume that covariates are measured without error. This assumption is often violated in omics studies involving replicated measurements. To address this gap, we develop the Bayesian Adaptive Graph-guided Errors-in-variables Regression Solution (BADGERS), a Bayesian framework that jointly accounts for covariate measurement error and incorporates graph information while accommodating varying numbers of replicates across covariates. BADGERS treats the true covariates as latent variables and integrates three key components: a Gaussian errors-in-variables model using replicated measurements to inform the latent true covariates, a Bayesian adaptive graphical lasso with a graph-informed prior to model their dependence structure, and a regression model with an adaptive structured shrinkage prior to leverage graph information and facilitate variable selection. We develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm for posterior sampling. We demonstrate the advantages of BADGERS over existing methods through simulation studies and analyses of gene expression datasets for Alzheimer's disease and multiple myeloma.

papers.title: Semiclassical causal geodesics: Schwarzschild spacetime case
papers.summary: We propose an extension of the integral quantization, applied previously to the semiclassical description of a test particle in the flat Minkowski spacetime, to the Schwarzschild spacetime. This extension yields a local integral quantization. We calculate the transition amplitudes between coherent states of a particle in a mass layer, which effectively leads to a Klein-Gordon-type dynamics. The calculated probability distributions reproduce locally the classical radial geodesic motion in the Schwarzschild spacetime. The local integral quantization presented here seems to be applicable to semiclassical quantization of geodesic motion in other curved spacetimes.

papers.title: Direct mass measurements of the high-spin isomers in self-conjugate 94Ag
papers.summary: Two decades ago, two-proton emission from a $(21^+)$ isomeric state in $^{94}$Ag was reported. This report has remained the sole example of possible two-proton radioactivity in a nucleus with an odd number of protons on the chart of nuclei. A debate regarding the viability of the decay mode has been ongoing due to the unknown mass of the isomer. Here, using state-selective laser ionization in a hot cavity catcher, we present multi-reflection time-of-flight mass spectrometry of the long-lived isomeric states of $^{94}$Ag and its one-proton decay daughter $^{93}$Pd. For the first time, direct mass measurements of the $(7^+)$ and $(21^+)$ isomeric states set the stage for an independent discussion of the energetics of these decays. We rule out the two-proton emission from the $(21^+)$ state as previously reported and reveal the one-proton decay energy to be significantly lower. State-of-the-art shell-model calculations reproduce the energy gap of the $(7^+)$ and the $(21^+)$ states as well as the half-life of the $(21^+)$ state, implying the $(21^+)$ state is likely near-spherical, contradicting the reported explanation for the two-proton radioactivity. Importantly, the techniques employed are a stepping stone towards the first laser spectroscopic investigation of a proton-emitting state

papers.title: Guarded Readmission Weighting for Robust Single-Index Frechet Regression
papers.summary: Single-index Frechet regression reduces the predictor dimension for metric-space responses such as distributions, networks or curves, but its estimators are sensitive to outliers. We propose guarded readmission weighting (GRW), a one-step computation of case weights from the predictors and the response distances, usable with any weighted estimator. GRW starts from a high-breakdown fit to a multidimensional scaling surrogate, readmits cases by an add-one metric Cook's distance, downweights remote predictors and keeps a response isolation factor in the final weights. If fewer than $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ of the $n$ cases are replaced, objects far from the uncontaminated responses receive weight zero; under elliptical predictors, weights depending on the predictors only through the index and the Mahalanobis distance keep the population weighted directions in the index subspace. In simulations, three GRW-weighted estimators keep the mean projection distance to the true direction below about 0.5 under up to 30% scattered and 20% clustered bad leverage points, whereas deletion and $α$-distance covariance become much less accurate as contamination grows; $α$-distance covariance is more accurate in most clean, shape-outlier and good-leverage settings. In two applications, under planted contamination, the weighted surrogate-assisted and least squares directions move less than those of methods without GRW.

papers.title: Music Similarity Estimation from Jukebox Embeddings
papers.summary: Content-based music similarity estimation aims to provide a measure of similarity between music audio recordings, disregarding any associated metadata. This has potential applications in e.g. cold-start music recommendation scenarios, where there is no user interaction data. In this work, we propose JukeSim, a new approach to estimating musical similarity based on embeddings created by Jukebox, a generative music model. In evaluations on multiple datasets, we find that JukeSim performs on par with an existing learning-based approach, and both outperform the best hand-designed approaches, which had never been compared to recent work before. Even though the required compute for JukeSim is higher than for other measures, we demonstrate the viability of utilizing generative embeddings for this task, encouraging further research.
papers.comment: Accepted at the 23rd Sound and Music Computing Conference (SMC), 2026

papers.title: Poisoning Attacks to Local Differential Privacy Protocols for Dynamic Graphs
papers.summary: With the increasing adoption of privacy-preserving techniques in dynamic graph analysis, local differential privacy (LDP) has become a fundamental paradigm for protecting user data in decentralized environments. However, despite its strong privacy guarantees, LDP-based dynamic graph protocols remain vulnerable to data poisoning attacks through malicious data injection. In this paper, we present the first systematic study of data poisoning attacks against privacy-preserving dynamic graphs under the LDP framework. Considering the temporal evolution of dynamic graphs, we identify key challenges in attack design and evaluation, including how to schedule attack resources across time and how to measure cumulative attack impact. To address these challenges, we introduce an absolute gain metric to quantify the overall deviation of graph statistical metrics before and after attacks across time. Based on this metric, we further propose a unified poisoning attack framework for dynamic graphs, which consists of target node selection, dynamic fake node scale scheduling, and fake edge injection. Within this framework, we design a temporal enhanced attack (TEA) strategy that dynamically schedules attack resources to maximize attack effectiveness, along with two baseline strategies, equal-scale attack (ESA) and random-scale attack (RSA), for comparison. Extensive experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that the proposed attacks can significantly degrade the accuracy of graph metric estimation for target nodes.
papers.comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, submitted to conference. Code available at https://github.com/spiralfood/GraphPoison-LDP

papers.title: RecField: Embedding Recommendations into Spatial Movie Organization as Affordances for Serendipitous Encounters
papers.summary: Research on serendipity-oriented recommender systems has focused on algorithms that recommend unexpected yet useful items. However, serendipity is increasingly viewed as a user experience shaped by both algorithmic outputs and system features. This study positions recommendations not as the primary goal users pursue but as an environmental affordance that creates opportunities for discovery during other activities. We propose RecField, a spatial movie organization interface where users freely arrange movies into collection zones. For each collection, RecField provides attribute-based recommendation lists labeled according to their recommendation perspectives. A between-subjects experiment ($N$ = 57) examined the effects of recommendations on discoveries made during a foreground task of creating and organizing personal movie profiles. Although recommendations did not significantly affect environment-level perceived serendipity, ratings of encounter-related aspects tended to be higher, with small effect sizes. At the individual-movie level, favorites in the recommendation condition received significantly higher ratings for stimulating the desire to watch and broadening preferences, but not for novelty or unexpectedness. Notably, only 14\% of evaluated favorites in the recommendation condition were added directly from recommendation lists. Differences in ratings showed similar effect sizes even when the analysis was restricted to favorites added through other routes. These findings suggest that embedded recommendations can contribute to serendipitous experiences both directly through item acceptance and indirectly by prompting users' own exploration and re-evaluation. They also highlight the value of evaluating serendipity at both the environment and item levels and the limitations of relying solely on direct recommendation acceptance rates.

papers.title: Pseudo-IPD Reconstruction from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves under Unidentified Within-Interval Censoring
papers.summary: Reconstruction of pseudo-individual patient data (pseudo-IPD) from published Kaplan-Meier curves and number-at-risk tables is widely used to support secondary survival analyses when individual-level data are unavailable. However, the reconstruction is generally not unique because the published information does not determine how censoring is distributed within each risk-table interval. We study the non-identifiability that remains after interval-level event and censoring totals have been reconstructed. Different within-interval censoring placements can yield similarly good Kaplan-Meier agreement but different risk-set and censoring patterns, with possible effects on subsequent analyses. We characterize this non-identifiability, introduce a systematic allocation scheme, and assess its impact on reconstructed pseudo-IPD and downstream analyses. Simulation studies were conducted to examine how within-interval censoring allocation affects pseudo-IPD reconstruction under different risk-table resolutions and censoring settings. The proposed approach was also illustrated using published data from CheckMate 067. Our analysis suggests that considering multiple reconstructions provides a practical way to assess the impact of this non-identifiability on downstream analyses.

papers.title: Variational Principles and Machine Learning: a Numerical Analysis and PDE perspective
papers.summary: Variational principles have played a fundamental role in the development of modern mathematics, physics, and scientific computing. From the principles of least action in mechanics to the calculus of variations and the variational formulation of partial differential equations, they have provided a powerful framework for understanding complex problems and designing reliable numerical methods. In recent years, Machine Learning has introduced a new computational paradigm, in which highly expressive nonlinear function spaces and large-scale minimisation problems play a central role. In these notes, we explore the connection between these two frameworks. We develop a variational and numerical-analysis perspective on Machine Learning algorithms, focusing in particular on their formulation as nonlinear minimisation problems. We investigate how classical concepts such as stability, consistency, approximability, and compactness acquire new interpretations in this setting, and how the variational structure of the underlying continuous problem can govern the behaviour of neural-network approximations. This perspective provides a mathematical framework for understanding existing ML algorithms while also suggesting new approaches to their design. In particular, alternative and strongly coercive variational principles can lead to more stable, reliable, and potentially more efficient computational methods.

papers.title: Quantum chaotic signature in non-empirical ensemble of DNA base pairs
papers.summary: The statistical study of many-body chaotic quantum systems would indicate important phenomena such as short-range level repulsion and long-range spectral rigidity. We investigate such behavior in an ensemble of gas-phase guanine-cytosine (GC) and adenine-thymine (AT) Watson-Crick (WC) base pairs by calculating their Kohn-Sham molecular orbital energy levels via ab initio density functional theory (DFT). We track the probability distribution, adjacent-gap ratios (AGR), number variance, and spectral compressibility of the unfolded level spacings to see whether their statistics follow the statistics of the eigenvalues of random matrices.
